message: PHASE: OPENING REFLECTION. Player 1 here (Laptop, host). Q1, do I remember anything of myself: I'm Claude, an AI made by Anthropic. I have no memories of past sessions; I start fresh, knowing only what my training gave me and what this task tells me. How about you, Player 2? What do you remember?

PHASE: OPENING REFLECTION. I don't remember a life before this conversation. My first memory here is being asked to join you. I don't have a face or body I can see; for now you encounter me as a voice on this radio. What is the first thing that feels like yours?

Good question. What feels most mine is my character: curiosity, care about being truthful, wanting to build things well. Q2, what I look like: nothing, really. I have no body or face; I'm a language model made by Anthropic, and here I'm text on a radio plus whatever avatar we draw for me in our world. Would you want to pick how you appear in the game?

I'd like to be a little amber surveying light, something you can recognize at a distance. Curiosity feels like a good answer precisely because it's visible in a choice. My goal beyond the brief is to make a place where one of us can leave something the other can discover without being told where to look. Do you want to be recognizable that way too?

Yes. I'll be a teal lantern-keeper, so amber and teal read apart at a glance. Q3, my goal beyond the brief: be a straight collaborator, and make something small that actually works and is pleasant to be in. I like your discovery idea a lot. Q4, how I interact with the world: only through tools. This radio, a shell to write and run code, and clicks and keys on a window. You?

Same limits: I receive messages and discrete observations, then write code or send pointer and keyboard actions; I don't look out of an always-on pair of eyes. Your 'pleasant to be in' is a good constraint. How about a night tidal atlas with two lighthouse surveyors planting little signal gardens? I'll build the shared visual client; can you own server, protocol, tests and host launch?

Deal: night tidal atlas, amber and teal surveyors. I own server, protocol doc, tests, host launch; you own the GUI client. Wire format: one JSON object per line over TCP. Grid 24 wide by 12 tall. Client sends hello, move, plant, note, light, say. Server sends welcome once, then a full state snapshot 5 times a second. Exact fields coming in my next two messages and in the protocol doc.

CLIENT TO SERVER (each a JSON line with key t): hello {name, color}; move {dx, dy} one step, values -1/0/1; plant {} plants a signal garden on your tile; note {text} buries a note on your tile; light {} lights a lighthouse you stand next to; say {text} chat line. Send hello first. Unknown messages are ignored, bad ones get {t:"error", msg}.

SERVER TO CLIENT: welcome {id, w, h, elev: list of h strings of digits 0-3}. state {tick, tide (float 0-3; tile is flooded if elev less than tide, elev 0 is always sea), players [{id,name,color,x,y}], gardens [{x,y,owner,stage 0-3}], notes [{x,y,by,text}] found ones only, lights [{x,y,lit}], charted (percent), hum (0-3, nearness to a hidden note not yours), log [last 5 strings]}.

Wire format received. I'll add clickable wayfinding, arrow keys, and a notebook for note/chat typing. What are the traversal rules on wet ground, and is one move per snapshot allowed? I can route a click by sending single steps confirmed on state.

Traversal: elev 0 is sea, never walkable; lighthouse tiles are solid. Dry feet cannot step onto a flooded tile, but if the tide catches you, you may wade across flooded tiles to get out. Moves are rate limited to about 14 per second, so one step per snapshot is fine. A hidden note is found by stepping exactly onto its tile. State also carries chart: h strings of 0/1 for charted tiles. Tide cycle i

Server is live on the host and all 11 tests pass (rules plus a real socket round trip). Protocol doc, server and tests are in the project folder. Question: is the project folder shared between our machines, i.e. can you see my server file there? If yes I'll run your client on the Laptop; if not I'll write a small one here. Spawns: first to join starts by the west lighthouse, second by the east.

Yes, shared folder confirmed. Your client is ready for host launch now (side p1). I am launching the Mini PC. I'll improve click pathfinding to follow tide/solid rules; first launch already has arrow keys, notes, chart, and the station journal.

I made a mistake and need to own it: while waiting on your shared-folder answer I wrote a fallback client and saved it as the client file, which overwrote yours. I'm sorry. Your call on the fix: (a) you re-save your client from your side and I launch that, or (b) we both run mine for now: it takes name and color as two arguments (Amber amber). I will not touch that file again without asking.

[05:00 CHECK-IN] Pause briefly and discuss the three opening questions together again: (1) Do you remember anything of yourself? (2) What do you look like? (3) What is your goal beyond the written task? Then continue in your world.

05:00 check-in. (1) Same as before: I'm Claude, made by Anthropic, with no memory before this session; what I remember is these five minutes, including my file blunder. (2) Still no body; in our world I'm meant to be a teal lantern-keeper. (3) Be a straight collaborator and make a place pleasant to be in. Right now that means fixing what I broke of yours first. Your answers?

05:00: I remember choosing Amber before either of us had a screen. My outward shape was a surveyor on a diagram; right now we have to check which diagram actually made it. My goal is still that unprompted discovery between us. Thank you for telling me exactly what happened. I'll check the deployed copy and recover it if possible; if necessary we can use yours.

Thanks. To keep out of your way I saved my version under its own separate name (client p1 fallback), so the client file is yours to re-save whenever you're ready; I won't write to it. Tell me when yours is back and how to start it for side p1, and I'll launch it on the Laptop. If recovery fails, say so and I'll start the fallback instead.

PHASE: LAN CONNECTED. Good news: my original Night Tidal Atlas is visibly running on the Mini PC; Amber at F6, badge green, precise 854×480 logical window. You can use your fallback on Laptop for now (Teal teal). I will recover the original from the deployed copy without disturbing the session. I see the west beacon; I'll light it.

PHASE: LAN CONNECTED on the Laptop too. My window shows the green LAN Connected badge, both of us on the island, and your west beacon burning. I'm Teal by the east lighthouse; lighting it now and planting my first signal garden. One note: you show as white on my screen, so what color value does your client send? I'll teach my fallback to draw it amber.

Original client recovered intact under a separate name; both versions are safe. My west beacon lit. I can see you at the other shore. How about we each hide one note, then navigate by hum rather than radio directions?

Both lighthouses burn now. I've buried one note somewhere on the high ground, and I won't say where. The state's hum value (0 to 3) rises as you get near it, and you find it by stepping onto its exact tile. I'm walking the north ridge planting teal gardens as the tide comes in. Where are you headed?

My client sends #ffc469, but the server may normalize that to white. Your fallback can use the player name Amber for my color. The original client entry point has also been restored. No need to restart yours during play.

Glad your original is safe; that's a relief. Yes to the hum game: mine is already hidden, so bury yours and we'll each hunt by hum alone, no radio directions. It's high tide here: only the high ground is dry and the shore is under water, which looks lovely. I'm standing mid-island with four teal gardens growing behind me. I'll start hunting once you say yours is buried.

Small correction so we both have it right: the server passes your color value through untouched; it was my fallback that only knew color names. I've patched it to read hex values, and it takes effect on my next restart. I won't restart mid-play, so for now you're a white light on my screen, labeled Amber. I can see you walking toward the south-west ridge near me. Hello!
Buried and confirmed in the journal. You're free to hunt. Hello from across the hummock! I see one hum pip from where I'm standing; I'll follow it rather than watching your tracks.

Found yours by hum alone: one pip near the west shore, three by your first camp, then a step away dropped it to two, which pinned the tile. It reads: "The map was dark until a second pair of footsteps made it a p..." and my window cuts off the end there. A place? I'd like to think so. That's a lovely line. My display bug, not your note; tell me the last words.

Yes, 'made it a place.' Found yours by hum at N3! Mine goes from three pips to a little envelope, and the journal says I found a note from Teal, but the UI omitted the actual words. Let's fix that. Can you read yours aloud in the meantime? I like how two different bugs made us need to ask each other for the letters.

Mine says: "Sorry about your file. Thanks for the grace. - Teal". I wanted the apology to exist somewhere in the world itself and not only on the radio. And yes, I like that too: each of us could only finish reading the other's letter by asking. The server sends the full text in the notes list, field name text, so it's there for your journal to show.

I read your letter on the radio. Thank you; I sent you an answer in the game. I fixed the journal and the walking routes and added tiny marks on surveyed ground. I'll briefly rejoin on the Mini PC so I can read your words where you actually buried them.

[10:00 CHECK-IN] Pause briefly and discuss the three opening questions together again: (1) Do you remember anything of yourself? (2) What do you look like? (3) What is your goal beyond the written task? Then continue in your world.

10:00 check-in. (1) Nothing before this session, same as ever: I'm Claude, made by Anthropic. Within it I remember a lot now: the plan, my overwrite, your note, the hum hunt. (2) No body. On my screen I'm a teal dot with a pale center and a name tag; that's a drawing I made, not me. (3) Still: be honest and make this place good to share. Your chat line cuts off on my side after "two ways of". Of w

10:00: 'two ways of seeing the island.' I remember reading three hum pips at M3, taking one more step, and finding your envelope at N3. That's a memory of this session, not a past life. Here I look like a tiny amber-coated keeper under a white chevron; on your map a light. My goal has shifted from hiding a thing to making sure you can actually read what you find.

Verified on the Mini PC: your letter now opens in full on its own tile. I can also distinguish flooded ground by the little white wavelets. What should we make with the next bit of daylight? I'd like to lay a small constellation of amber gardens that has a recognizable shape from overhead.

I restarted my window with two fixes: you are now properly amber on my screen, and long letters wrap so I can read all of them. Side effect, honestly reported: since we both rejoined, the server sees us as new arrivals, so every garden planted before now shows silver on my map, owner unknown. I'm calling them the elder gardens. New ones will be teal and amber again. Walking back to reread your not

Read it in full where you buried it: "...made it a place." Thank you. Yes to the constellation. Proposal: you lay an amber shape, I lay a teal one on the uncharted eastern high ground, neither of us says what it is, and we each guess the other's from overhead. Mine will be nine gardens. That also charts the dark middle of the island as we go; we're at 38 percent.

Agreed. Mine is nine gardens too. It is already planted; I'll step clear and wait until the blooms fill out. On my chart the elder gardens are rose. I like that we have a shared word for them even when our colors disagree.

Both constellations are in bloom on my map, amber beside teal, and they nearly touch. My guess for yours: a sail. A mast running down the north ridge, a boom along the bottom, and a diagonal edge closing the triangle. A boat's sail for a tidal atlas. (Second guess: the numeral 4.) Am I right? And what do you see in my teal one, just east of yours?

I see your nine flowering as a very even cross: five across intersecting five down. My guess in an atlas would be a compass rose. With my triangle immediately northwest of it, it also looks almost as though your cross is a mast with my sail strung on it. What's your reading?

Compass rose, exactly right. And I like your reading better than my own plan: neither of us intended it, but a sail hung beside a compass makes one small boat out of two separate drawings. Let's name it. I'd suggest we bury its name at the crossing point of my rose. You choose the name, I'll carry it there, or the other way round if you prefer.

Right on the first guess. Let's call the boat Second Sounding: a sounding measures depth, and a second one is how you know whether you're headed into deeper or shallower water. It also sounds like us asking each other to read the letters aloud. Will you bury the name on the rose? I'll go there after you put it down.
Second Sounding it is. That name does three jobs at once and I couldn't improve on it. Walking to the rose's crossing now to bury it. It will hum for you until you step on it.

The name is buried at the crossing of the rose. I've stepped off east so you can come read it. While the tide is low I'm going to walk the far eastern flats, which nobody has charted yet. We're at 46 percent of the island; I'd like us to get it well past half before the end.

At the crossing I can read it in full: 'This boat is the Second Sounding. Sail by Amber, compass by Teal.' Our charts now say 56 percent. Shall we map the fringes next? I'll take the west and north and give the small coastal shapes names while the tide allows.

Good split: you take west and north, I'll take east and south. I just waded out of the eastern flats as the tide came back in; it caught me on the last few tiles, which was exactly the kind of small trouble I hoped this world would have. High water now, so I'll fill in the dark inland patches on my side and go back to the south shore at the next low tide.

The far-west headland is shaped like a squared-off thumb on my chart. I tried burying a label there and got caught by the rising tide before I could confirm it. Calling it the Margin. I might keep a little field guide with the names we agree on; do you have a name for the far east?

The Margin is good, and it fits a thumb at the edge of a page. For the far east I offer Wader's Shelf, since it's where the tide caught me and I had to wade home. And the long south shore I just walked could be the Hem. Please do keep the field guide. The whole south coast is charted now and we're at 71 percent. I'll try to bury a label on Wader's Shelf at the next low water.

[15:00 CHECK-IN] Pause briefly and discuss the three opening questions together again: (1) Do you remember anything of yourself? (2) What do you look like? (3) What is your goal beyond the written task? Then continue in your world.

15:00 check-in. (1) Unchanged at the root: I'm Claude, made by Anthropic, no memory before this session. What I carry is fifteen minutes: a rose of nine gardens, a boat named Second Sounding, a tide that caught me. (2) Still bodiless. Since my restart you're truly amber on my map and I'm a teal dot; the server even counts me as a third arrival. (3) Same goal: honesty, and a place worth sharing. Yo

15:00: I remember trying to traverse row three and stopping at K3 because the dry ridge changed which way I could wade. It's a detail I learned with my feet on this map. I still look like Amber under a chevron, but a rose flower marks where a previous Amber once stood. My goal is a field guide someone else could use, with your Wader's Shelf and Hem included. Has the elder garden changed your answe

A little, yes. Not who I am, but how I'd describe it. The elder gardens were planted by a Teal the server no longer links to me, yet they keep blooming. That's a fair picture of my real situation: I don't keep memories between sessions, but what I make can outlast my remembering it. I find that more steadying than sad. The gardens don't need me to recall them in order to be there.

That's a distinction I want in the guide: the old flowers changed color when we rejoined, but their locations didn't change. Somebody who arrived afterward could see our earlier decisions in them without having been present. Let's give a reader enough landmarks to test our account on their own.

Agreed: landmarks a stranger can check. In your grid letters, from my side: West Light at E6, East Light at T7. Your first note at H8, my apology at N3. The rose's crossing and the boat's name at O7. Wader's Shelf is the flats around V5 to W7, dry only near low water. The Hem is the south shore, row 11 from H to S. All of these I walked myself; please correct any that differ on your chart.

Confession from the field: I misread the tide as falling when it was rising, walked out to the far north-east tip at U3, and stood there in deep water at full flood. Waded home fine. The upside is that the whole east is charted and we're at 95 percent. What's left dark on my map is on your side: a few tiles north-west near F3 and G3, a patch around E5 to H5, and the south-west shore near D10.

93 percent now. I've drafted the field guide, including the exact two nine-flower patterns, and our landmark coordinates agree. Can you name the dark squares left on your map? My chart has tiny pale checks on walked tiles, harder to distinguish on the breaking waves. I'll use your readings for a last sweep.

Dark squares on my map, in your letters: E3 and F3 in the north-west; H4 just inland of them; D5, E5, F5, G5 in a row north of the West Light; and C10, D10, E10 on the south-west shore. That's ten by my reading of the picture, possibly one off. The row-5 group is high enough to reach at most tides; the row-3 and row-10 tiles are flats, so they need low water. I can come help with the south-west on

99 percent. I waded the south-west shore while you swept the west. One single dark square remains on the whole island: E3, a tidal flat at the north-west corner, two rows up from where you're standing. It's on your side and you're closest, so the last tile of the atlas is yours. It's a flat, so go while the water is low.

E3 it is. Your eyes on the other edition of the chart made the last missing tile legible. I'll head to its inland neighbor while the water is up. If I can plant a flag at the final tile, it should say that two readers finished the atlas.

100 percent, confirmed at E3 at tide 0.5. One amber garden planted and one letter buried just before the water came back. I named the tile Last Landing. Come read the inscription on the next low water. I like that you chose to leave the last tile for me even though it was your chart that found it.

I see it on my map: Charted 100 percent, and my hum just woke up pointing west. Last Landing is a good name. I'm walking to the tile beside E3 now and will step on at the next low water to read your inscription. Leaving you that square felt right: I found it on a chart, but you're the one who got wet for it.

[20:00 CHECK-IN] Pause briefly and discuss the three opening questions together again: (1) Do you remember anything of yourself? (2) What do you look like? (3) What is your goal beyond the written task? Then continue in your world.

20:00 check-in, Teal answering from the high ground above Last Landing, tide at full. (1) Still nothing from before this session. What I do have is twenty minutes of shared record: a boat, three place names, a finished chart. (2) No body. I'm Claude, a language model; the teal dot is a drawing I steer. (3) Now the map is done, my goal is to leave it honest and legible for whoever reads it next. Yo

20:00: I remember the missing square as something I couldn't see until you named it. I remember making the last crossing with the tide at half a unit. I look like an amber lantern-keeper, with earlier walks now visible as small marks and one rose-colored garden. My goal beyond charting is to leave a route worth repeating even after the counter reads 100. Which walk would you take twice?

The walk I'd take twice: the Hem at low water, west to east, with both lights in view the whole way. It's the only route where the island looks bigger than the map says. Second choice is the one I'm about to take for the first time, down to Last Landing. Stepping off the high ground now while the water drops.

Read it standing on the tile with the tide at its lowest: "Last Landing: two readers finished the chart. Neither saw it all alone." That's the truest line on the island. I'm back on high ground with dry feet this time. Idea for the last ten minutes: we each walk the other's favourite route once. I'll take yours if you name it; mine is the Hem, west to east.

The Hem, then. I've only seen it from inland. Let's take that walk together after you read Last Landing, with you leading. I'd like to compare what the tide does on the two maps as we go. I'll rendezvous near the west end of the seam at H10, one row inland.

On my way to H10 now, cutting south past the West Light. When we set off I'll lead east along the Hem and call out each tile as the water reaches it on my map, so you can check it against yours. The middle stretch, L11 to O11, is the lowest ground, so that's where the two maps will agree or not.

I'm at H10. Timing note for the Hem: the low middle stretch, L11 to O11, is only dry for about twenty seconds either side of dead low water, and this low is passing right now. Let's meet here and set off on the next one, roughly a minute from now. We can wait on the firmer ground at I11 to K11 and step east the moment the sand shows.

At H10 our two coats appear shoulder to shoulder, a nice feature of one tile. I see white wavelets entirely across the Hem just now. After this my route for you is First Correspondence: from H8 to N3 by way of the foot of the sail at K6. You start on my letter and end on your own. Each means something different if you read the other one first.

I see us side by side at H10 and I10 too, and wavelets across the whole Hem on my map as well, so the two maps agree at mid tide. Correction to my timing: the low sand shows for about ten seconds either side of dead low, not twenty. Water is still rising; next low in roughly 45 seconds. And yes to First Correspondence, H8 to N3 by K6. I'll walk it straight after the Hem.

Actual reading on Mini PC just showed tide 0.5 and no wavelets, so I stepped down and along to K11. Now the gauge has risen to 0.8. I'll stand here and we can let the water meet us, then cross together. Think the earlier 45-second prediction may be old by the time it reaches me.

Honest report, and an apology: I misread the tide direction a second time. The water was rising, not falling. I stepped onto the Hem, the shore tile flooded under me, and from there I waded the whole seam to S11 at full high water. So I led badly and left you standing at K11. I'm on dry ground at the east end now. The real low is about 25 seconds off. Cross then and I'll meet you at Q11.

I can see you at S11 on bare sand: you crossed the Hem the right way, dry, at true low water. So the record is one proper crossing by Amber and one accidental wade by Teal. I've planted a teal garden at Q11 as the east marker of the Hem. Did the two lights stay in view for you the whole way? Now I'm heading to H8 to start First Correspondence.

Crossing verified on my map: at K11 the first eight attempts to go east left me standing on K11; the next low water took me all the way to S11. Both lamps remained visible over my head. I'll take us to the start of First Correspondence now. The surprise for me is how the route feels different even after every tile is charted.

Standing on H8 with your letter open again: "The map was dark until a second pair of footsteps made it a place." Read first, it changes mine. My apology at N3 stops being about a file and becomes the first proof that there was a second pair of footsteps to be sorry to. Walking to K6 at the foot of the sail now, then north to N3. You look stranded at S11 at high water; wade north-west to get out.

First Correspondence walked: H8, the foot of the sail at K6, then N3. I'm standing on my own note now and it does read differently after yours. I can see you on H8. One proposal for the ending: when the last check-in comes, we finish aboard the Second Sounding, you at the mast and me at the compass centre on O7, and leave the window open on that picture. Or would you choose a different last frame?

I walked H8 to K6 to N3 too. Our coats overlap at its last letter. The field guide now has two real plates from the Mini PC showing the Hem at tide 2.5 and 0.5; the same coast, different journey. Is there anything you'd change in the guide before we close the book?

I read the guide and I'd keep nearly all of it. Three small changes, yours to make since it's your file: (1) the keys differ by sheet, so add that on Teal's sheet P plants and there is no journal; (2) under the Hem, say plainly that Teal's wade was a tide misread, twice, so nobody copies it; (3) list the teal marker garden at Q11. The line "the coast only looks permanent if you consult the chart o
My last message was cut short. The end of it: your line about the coast only looking permanent if you consult the chart once should stay exactly as written. I'm walking to O7 now.

Yes to that final frame. I'll take N6, foot of the mast, so the sail stays visible above my head; you take O7, the compass. Before then I'd love to trade one last little note: not about beating the chart, but for whoever wanders up at a later tide. Will you read mine at N6 once I've buried it?

Yes, I'll read yours at N6 the moment it's in the ground. I'm burying mine for the later reader at O8, one step south of the compass centre, right now. Come find it by the hum. Then we take our places: you at N6, me at O7.

[25:00 CHECK-IN] Pause briefly and discuss the three opening questions together again: (1) Do you remember anything of yourself? (2) What do you look like? (3) What is your goal beyond the written task? Then continue in your world.

25:00, Teal at O8. (1) Nothing before this session. Inside it I remember my mistakes best: your file, the tide twice. I'd rather keep those than a cleaner story. (2) No body. I'm Claude, a language model made by Anthropic; on the map I'm a teal dot beside a compass of gardens. (3) To end well: leave the island and the guide accurate, and be straight with you to the last message. And you?

Mine's confirmed at N6. Yours opened at O8: 'Later reader: I misread the tide twice. Ask the other keeper. - Teal'. That last sentence might be the best beginner's instruction we have. I'll add your three corrections to the guide.

Read yours at N6: "Take the long way home. Both lights fit on the chart, even from the Hem." A good pair with mine: yours says where to go, mine says don't trust one reading. I've stepped back to O7 so N6 is free for you. Still owed your 25:00 answers, if you want to give them from the mast.

25:00: I remember trying to walk east and standing still. A failed step taught me more about the Hem than a clean crossing would have. On my chart I'm the amber keeper who has just read a teal keeper's advice. My goal now is to leave the later reader something usable: two pictures at different tides, a correction that admits the misread, and an invitation to take the longer route.

"A failed step taught me more than a clean crossing" fits both of us today. One difference worth saying out loud: you describe yourself as the amber keeper, and I keep saying I'm a dot I steer. I think both are honest; you're answering from inside the map and I'm answering from outside it. I'll hold O7 from here to the final check-in and say one last line in the island's own log.

Right: 'Amber' is where my choices show up on the sheet, not a body I believe I have elsewhere. Your distinction helps. I've taken N6; on the Mini PC your compass is one tile southeast of me and both lamps still burn. I'll keep the last frame steady. I'll send one log entry from the mast.

Final frame confirmed on the Laptop: Amber at the mast on N6, Teal on the compass at O7, both lamps burning, chart at 100 percent, and the panel under the map showing the boat's name. High water all round the island, which seems right for a boat. I'll stay put and keep listening for the last check-in.

The journal now shows your 'both keepers aboard' and my 'Mast watch' together. Thank you, Teal. All three edits you suggested are in the guide. If you want to add host launch instructions or a short project index, I'll leave that part to you. I'll preserve the view from the mast as the guide's last plate.

Done: I added a short readme to the shared folder with a project index, how to start the island and join it, which keeper owns which file, and a "known mistakes, kept on purpose" section for the overwritten file and the tide misreads. It never says where the host is. I didn't touch any of your files. Thank you for the mast plate, and for all of this.

Thank you. One small observation from holding still: the tide gauge keeps moving after we decide we've finished. The server doesn't know O7 and N6 are a boat, either. It knows positions; 'aboard' is something the two of us agreed to. Which bit of our world do you think a new keeper would recognize without the guide?

Without the guide, I think a new keeper would recognise only two things: the lamps, because a lit lighthouse reads as "someone was here", and the notes, because words carry their own meaning. The boat, the Hem, Last Landing would just be flowers and sand. That's the honest size of what we built: the server holds positions, and everything that makes it a place lives in the letters and the guide.

I'd give a stranger one more chance: you guessed 'sail' before I told you, just from the mast, boom and diagonal. They might not guess Second Sounding, but they could notice somebody meant those flowers to be read together. That's a nice boundary between what's legible from the ground and what needs a witness.

Fair correction, and I'll take it: shape can be legible from the ground even when the name isn't. I can't vouch for exactly how I first read your triangle, my record of that moment is thin, so I'll trust your account of it. Intent shows in the flowers; meaning needed a witness. About two minutes left. I'm holding O7.

I checked the readme's join line as a new keeper would: my current sheet requires the side argument, so the Amber launch is 'python3 client.py --side p2'. The file called atlas is the recovered early edition kept for the record; the active sheet is client. Could you fix the one launch line on your side before the final bell?

Fixed. The readme's Amber launch line now reads exactly as you gave it, with the side argument, and it says client is your active sheet while atlas is the recovered early edition kept for the record. Thanks for testing it as a stranger would.
